title: Foundations & Research Methods
subject: Psychology 101
description: What psychology is, how psychologists study it, and how to spot a solid claim.

questions.q: Which approach explains behavior through unconscious drives and early childhood experience?
questions.explain: Freud's psychoanalytic approach centers unconscious drives and early childhood.

questions.q: A researcher watches students in a cafeteria without interfering. This is:
questions.explain: Naturalistic observation means watching behavior in its natural setting without manipulating it.

questions.q: In an experiment, the variable the researcher deliberately changes is the:
questions.explain: The independent variable is manipulated; the dependent variable is measured.

questions.q: Which correlation shows the strongest relationship?
questions.explain: Strength is about distance from zero, not the sign: |-0.85| is the largest.

questions.q: A single, deep study of one unusual patient is called a:
questions.explain: Case studies examine one person or group in depth — rich detail, weak generalizability.

questions.q: Participants who unknowingly receive a fake treatment are in the:
questions.explain: A placebo is an inert treatment; the placebo group is the comparison for expectancy effects.

questions.q: Random assignment is used in experiments mainly to:
questions.explain: Random assignment distributes individual differences evenly so the IV is the likely cause of differences.

questions.q: The branch of psychology focused on mental processes like memory and problem-solving is:
questions.explain: Cognitive psychology studies how people perceive, remember, think, and solve problems.

questions.q: Which ethical rule requires explaining a study to participants afterward, especially after deception?
options: Debriefing is optional in all studies
questions.explain: Debriefing explains the study's true purpose and clears up any deception.

questions.q: Wilhelm Wundt is credited with:
questions.explain: Wundt opened the first psychology lab in Leipzig in 1879, marking psychology's start as a science.

rounds.title: Foundations & Research Methods
rounds.desc: What psychology is, how psychologists study it, and how to spot a solid claim.

title: Freud & Psychoanalysis
subject: Psychology 101
description: Id, ego, superego; psychosexual stages; how Freud thought personality is built.

questions.q: According to Freud, the part of personality that operates on the pleasure principle is the:
questions.explain: The id is present at birth and demands immediate gratification — the pleasure principle.

questions.q: The ego operates on which principle?
questions.explain: The ego mediates between the id and reality, delaying gratification when needed.

questions.q: The superego is best described as:
questions.explain: The superego holds internalized morals and ideals — it's where conscience lives.

questions.q: Freud's first psychosexual stage, focused on feeding, is the:
questions.explain: The oral stage (birth–~18 months) centers on the mouth: sucking and feeding.

questions.q: During which stage does Freud say sexuality goes dormant and children focus on school and peers?
questions.explain: Latency (roughly ages 6–puberty) is a quiet period — energy goes to skills and friendships.

questions.q: The Oedipus complex occurs during which stage?
questions.explain: In the phallic stage (ages 3–6), Freud claimed children desire the opposite-sex parent.

questions.q: When an adult gets stuck at a psychosexual stage, Freud called it:
questions.explain: Fixation is being stuck at a stage because of over- or under-gratification.

questions.q: Freud's method of having patients say whatever comes to mind is:
questions.explain: Free association lets uncensored thoughts reveal unconscious material.

questions.q: In therapy, when a patient redirects feelings about someone else onto the therapist, that's:
questions.explain: Transference is redirecting feelings from a significant person onto the analyst.

questions.q: Freud believed dreams were:
options: The royal road to the unconscious
questions.explain: Freud called dreams 'the royal road to the unconscious' — wishes disguised in symbols.

questions.q: The energy of the life instinct (libido) is said to drive which structure?
questions.explain: Libido is the psychic energy of the id's life instincts.

questions.q: Freud's three levels of consciousness were the conscious, preconscious, and:
questions.explain: The unconscious holds repressed drives and memories outside awareness (note: 'subconscious' is not a Freudian term).

rounds.title: Freud & Psychoanalysis
rounds.desc: Id, ego, superego; psychosexual stages; how Freud thought personality is built.

title: Defense Mechanisms
subject: Psychology 101
description: The ego's toolkit: spot each defense from a real-life scenario.

questions.q: After bombing an exam, Maya insists the professor 'has it out for her' and never considers that she didn't study. She is blaming her own failure on someone else — actually she's attributing her shortcomings to others. This is:
questions.explain: Projection: attributing your own unacceptable feelings or faults to someone else.

questions.q: A man furious at his boss comes home and snaps at his dog. This is:
questions.explain: Displacement redirects an impulse toward a safer target.

questions.q: An ex-smoker now lectures everyone about smoking and campaigns against it with unusual intensity. Freud would suspect:
questions.explain: Reaction formation: expressing the exact opposite of an unacceptable urge.

questions.q: A soldier recounts a traumatic battle in flat, purely factual detail, discussing strategy only. He is using:
questions.explain: Intellectualization avoids painful feelings by focusing on abstract, factual analysis.

questions.q: After a breakup, a student takes up boxing and channels everything into training. This healthy redirection is:
questions.explain: Sublimation channels unacceptable impulses into socially valued activities — Freud saw it as mature.

questions.q: A four-year-old who was toilet-trained starts wetting the bed after a new sibling arrives. This is:
questions.explain: Regression: returning to behavior from an earlier developmental stage under stress.

questions.q: A driver who caused an accident says 'well, the sun was in everyone's eyes, it could've happened to anybody.' This is:
questions.explain: Rationalization generates logical-sounding excuses to protect self-esteem.

questions.q: A woman cannot remember a genuinely traumatic childhood event at all — the memory is simply gone from awareness. The mechanism is:
questions.explain: Repression pushes threatening material out of conscious awareness entirely — Freud's foundational defense.

questions.q: A patient refuses to accept a serious diagnosis, insisting the labs 'must have mixed up the samples,' week after week. This is:
questions.explain: Denial is refusing to accept a painful reality.

questions.q: A shy student adopts the slang, style, and opinions of a popular athlete she admires, as if taking on his identity for protection. This is:
questions.explain: Identification: taking on the traits of someone more powerful or admired to bolster the self.

rounds.title: Defense Mechanisms
rounds.desc: The ego's toolkit: spot each defense from a real-life scenario.

title: Trait & Humanistic Personality
subject: Psychology 101
description: The Big Five, Maslow, Rogers, and the self — plus the biases that distort how we see ourselves.

questions.q: The Big Five factor 'O' stands for:
questions.explain: OCEAN: Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism.

questions.q: Someone who is organized, dependable, and disciplined scores high in:
questions.explain: Conscientiousness covers self-discipline, planning, and dependability.

questions.q: According to Maslow, the need at the very top of the hierarchy is:
questions.explain: Self-actualization — fulfilling your potential — sits at the top, after basic needs are met.

questions.q: Carl Rogers believed people flourish when they receive ___ from others.
questions.explain: Unconditional positive regard — acceptance without conditions — lets the self-concept grow.

questions.q: The gap between your actual self and your ideal self, in Rogers' terms, produces:
questions.explain: Incongruence is the mismatch between self-concept and experience/ideal, producing anxiety.

questions.q: Bandura's belief in your own ability to succeed at a task is called:
questions.explain: Self-efficacy is task-specific confidence, built through mastery, modeling, and encouragement.

questions.q: Rotter's 'locus of control': people who believe outcomes depend on their own actions have a(n):
questions.explain: Internal locus = 'my choices drive outcomes'; external = 'luck and others decide.'

questions.q: The tendency to attribute your successes to yourself but your failures to outside forces is the:
questions.explain: Self-serving bias protects self-esteem: wins are mine, losses are circumstances.

questions.q: Feeling like a fraud who will be 'found out' despite real accomplishments is the:
questions.explain: The imposter phenomenon: high achievers who can't internalize their success.

questions.q: BIRGing refers to:
options: Basking in reflected glory of a successful group
questions.explain: BIRGing = Basking In Reflected Glory — 'we won!' when your team wins, distance when it loses.

rounds.title: Trait & Humanistic Personality
rounds.desc: The Big Five, Maslow, Rogers, and the self — plus the biases that distort how we see ourselves.

title: Object Relations & Closing the Gaps
subject: Psychology 101
description: Klein, Winnicott, Mahler — and the exam details students most often miss.

questions.q: Object relations theory shifts focus from Freud's drives to:
questions.explain: Object relations theorists argued relationships — especially with early caregivers — shape personality.

questions.q: Melanie Klein is known for developing:
options: Play therapy with children and object relations ideas
questions.explain: Klein pioneered play therapy and argued infants form internal 'objects' from early experiences.

questions.q: Winnicott's term for a blanket or toy that comforts a child separating from a caregiver is:
questions.explain: A transitional object (like a blanket) helps the child bridge dependence and independence.

questions.q: Winnicott's 'good enough mother' refers to a caregiver who:
options: Never lets the child feel frustration
Is adequately responsive without being perfect
questions.explain: 'Good enough' care is responsive but imperfect — small frustrations help the child develop.

questions.q: Margaret Mahler's theory centers on:
options: Separation-individuation in the first years of life
questions.explain: Mahler described how infants psychologically 'hatch' from symbiosis into separate selves.

questions.q: In Mahler's phases, the period where infant and mother are experienced as one unit is:
questions.explain: Symbiosis (roughly months 1–5): the infant experiences no boundary between self and mother.

questions.q: A toddler who ventures off to explore, then returns to the caregiver for emotional 'refueling,' is in Mahler's:
questions.explain: Rapprochement: toddlers oscillate between independence and needing the caregiver close.

questions.q: Anna Freud is best known in personality theory for:
questions.explain: Anna Freud's 'The Ego and the Mechanisms of Defence' (1936) organized the defense mechanisms.

questions.q: Freud's genital stage begins at:
questions.explain: The genital stage starts at puberty, when sexual interests mature toward adult relationships.

questions.q: A patient unconsciously repeating childhood relationship patterns with the therapist is evidence of transference — the concept was central to which theorist's method?
questions.explain: Freud made transference a core tool of psychoanalytic treatment.

rounds.title: Object Relations & Closing the Gaps
rounds.desc: Klein, Winnicott, Mahler — and the exam details students most often miss.

title: Social Psychology Essentials
subject: Psychology 101
description: Attribution, conformity, obedience, and why groups change what we do.

questions.q: Overestimating personality and underestimating the situation when judging others is the:
questions.explain: The fundamental attribution error: we blame their character, excuse our own with circumstances.

questions.q: In Milgram's obedience studies, about what share of participants delivered the maximum shock?
questions.explain: Roughly 65% went to the maximum 450V when prompted by the experimenter.

questions.q: Asch's line studies demonstrated:
questions.explain: Asch showed people will give an obviously wrong answer to match a unanimous group.

questions.q: The presence of others making each person feel less responsible for helping is:
questions.explain: Diffusion of responsibility underlies the bystander effect — more witnesses, less help.

questions.q: When being watched improves performance on easy tasks but hurts on hard ones, that's:
questions.explain: Social facilitation: arousal from an audience boosts dominant (well-learned) responses.

questions.q: A group that suppresses dissent to preserve harmony, making a flawed decision, shows:
questions.explain: Groupthink: cohesion and pressure for unanimity override realistic appraisal.

questions.q: Cognitive dissonance is the discomfort from:
options: Holding two conflicting attitudes or acting against your beliefs
questions.explain: Festinger: inconsistency between attitudes and behavior creates pressure to change one of them.

questions.q: The foot-in-the-door technique works by:
options: Getting a small yes first, then asking for more
questions.explain: A small initial agreement makes a larger related request more likely to succeed.

questions.q: Prejudice is best defined as a(n):
options: Unjustified negative attitude toward a group
questions.explain: Prejudice = attitude; stereotype = belief; discrimination = behavior.

questions.q: Thinking your own good traits explain your success but your rival's success is luck is an example of:
questions.explain: Self-serving bias — the same pattern, applied to the comparison in the question.

rounds.title: Social Psychology Essentials
rounds.desc: Attribution, conformity, obedience, and why groups change what we do.

title: Cells & Energy
subject: Biology 101
description: Organelles, membranes, photosynthesis, and cellular respiration.

questions.q: Which organelle produces most of a cell's ATP?
questions.explain: Mitochondria run cellular respiration, producing most ATP.

questions.q: The cell membrane is mainly built from a bilayer of:
questions.explain: The phospholipid bilayer forms the membrane's basic structure.

questions.q: Photosynthesis takes place in the:
questions.explain: Chloroplasts capture light energy to build sugars.

questions.q: Which molecule is the cell's main energy currency?
questions.explain: ATP stores and releases energy for cellular work.

questions.q: Movement of water across a membrane from low to high solute concentration is:
questions.explain: Osmosis is water's diffusion across a selectively permeable membrane.

questions.q: Which structure makes proteins?
questions.explain: Ribosomes translate mRNA into proteins.

questions.q: Plant cells differ from animal cells because plant cells have:
questions.explain: Cell walls and chloroplasts are found in plant cells, not animal cells.

questions.q: The overall equation for cellular respiration produces:
questions.explain: Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + ATP energy.

questions.q: Enzymes speed up reactions by:
questions.explain: Enzymes lower the activation energy needed for a reaction.

questions.q: A solution with more solute than a cell, causing the cell to shrink, is:
questions.explain: Hypertonic solutions draw water out of the cell.

rounds.title: Cells & Energy
rounds.desc: Organelles, membranes, photosynthesis, and cellular respiration.

title: Genetics & Heredity
subject: Biology 101
description: DNA, Punnett squares, inheritance patterns, and mutations.

questions.q: The shape of DNA is a:
questions.explain: Watson and Crick's model: DNA is a double helix.

questions.q: In DNA, adenine (A) pairs with:
questions.explain: Base pairing: A–T and C–G in DNA.

questions.q: A genotype of two different alleles, like Bb, is called:
questions.explain: Heterozygous means two different alleles for a gene.

questions.q: Crossing Bb × Bb, roughly what fraction of offspring show the recessive trait?
questions.explain: Bb × Bb gives 1 BB : 2 Bb : 1 bb — 25% show the recessive phenotype.

questions.q: The process of copying DNA into RNA is:
questions.explain: Transcription makes RNA from a DNA template; translation builds protein.

questions.q: Which RNA carries amino acids to the ribosome?
questions.explain: Transfer RNA (tRNA) brings amino acids matched to codons.

questions.q: A change in a DNA sequence is called a:
questions.explain: Mutations are any changes to the DNA sequence.

questions.q: Humans normally have how many chromosomes in a body cell?
questions.explain: 46 chromosomes (23 pairs) in a typical human somatic cell.

questions.q: An allele that masks another allele is:
questions.explain: Dominant alleles are expressed even with one copy.

questions.q: When both alleles show up fully in the phenotype (like AB blood), it's:
questions.explain: Codominance: both traits appear, e.g., AB blood type.

rounds.title: Genetics & Heredity
rounds.desc: DNA, Punnett squares, inheritance patterns, and mutations.

title: Evolution & Natural Selection
subject: Biology 101
description: Darwin, adaptation, speciation, and evidence for evolution.

questions.q: Natural selection acts on which level?
questions.explain: Selection acts on phenotypes; evolution is the change in allele frequencies that follows.

questions.q: Structures with the same origin but different functions (bat wing, human arm) are:
questions.explain: Homologous structures share ancestry; analogous ones share function only.

questions.q: A trait that improves survival and reproduction is an:
questions.explain: Adaptations are heritable traits shaped by selection that aid fitness.

questions.q: When two populations can no longer interbreed, they are separate:
questions.explain: Reproductive isolation defines separate species under the biological species concept.

questions.q: Genetic drift has the biggest effect in:
questions.explain: Random changes matter most when the population is small.

questions.q: The raw material that natural selection works on comes from:
questions.explain: Without heritable variation, selection has nothing to act on.

questions.q: Darwin developed his theory partly from observing finches on the:
questions.explain: Galápagos finches' beaks varied by island and food source.

questions.q: A structure with no current function, like the human appendix, is called:
questions.explain: Vestigial structures are reduced remnants of ancestral features.

rounds.title: Evolution & Natural Selection
rounds.desc: Darwin, adaptation, speciation, and evidence for evolution.

title: Ecology Basics
subject: Biology 101
description: Food webs, cycles, populations, and how organisms interact.

questions.q: Organisms that make their own food are called:
questions.explain: Producers (autotrophs) capture energy, usually by photosynthesis.

questions.q: Roughly how much energy transfers from one trophic level to the next?
questions.explain: The 10% rule: most energy is lost as heat at each level.

questions.q: A relationship where both species benefit is:
questions.explain: Mutualism benefits both partners.

questions.q: The maximum population an environment can support long-term is its:
questions.explain: Carrying capacity is set by resources like food, water, and space.

questions.q: Bacteria that break down dead matter and return nutrients to soil are:
questions.explain: Decomposers recycle nutrients back into the ecosystem.

questions.q: Which cycle relies heavily on bacteria to fix an atmospheric gas into usable form?
questions.explain: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria convert N₂ into ammonia plants can use.

questions.q: When a predator and prey compete over the same limited resource, that's:
questions.explain: Competition between different species is interspecific.

questions.q: The first species to colonize bare rock after a disturbance are:
questions.explain: Pioneer species start ecological succession on bare surfaces.

rounds.title: Ecology Basics
rounds.desc: Food webs, cycles, populations, and how organisms interact.

title: Atoms & the Periodic Table
subject: Chemistry 101
description: Subatomic particles, atomic numbers, groups, and periods.

questions.q: The atomic number of an element equals its number of:
options: Electrons in the outer shell only
questions.explain: Atomic number = proton count, which defines the element.

questions.q: Which particle has a negative charge?
questions.explain: Electrons carry a −1 charge; protons +1; neutrons 0.

questions.q: Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons are:
questions.explain: Isotopes differ in neutrons, so they differ in mass.

questions.q: Elements in the same column of the periodic table share:
questions.explain: Groups (columns) share valence-electron patterns and similar behavior.

questions.q: How many electrons can the first shell hold?
questions.explain: The first shell holds a maximum of 2 electrons.

questions.q: Sodium (Na) has atomic number 11. A neutral sodium atom has how many electrons?
questions.explain: Neutral atoms have equal protons and electrons: 11.

questions.q: Which group contains the highly reactive alkali metals?
questions.explain: Group 1 (except hydrogen) are the alkali metals.

questions.q: The noble gases are known for being:
questions.explain: Full outer shells make noble gases very unreactive.

questions.q: An atom that gains or loses electrons becomes a(n):
questions.explain: Ions are charged atoms (or groups of atoms).

questions.q: The mass number equals protons plus:
questions.explain: Mass number = protons + neutrons.

rounds.title: Atoms & the Periodic Table
rounds.desc: Subatomic particles, atomic numbers, groups, and periods.

title: Bonding & Reactions
subject: Chemistry 101
description: Ionic vs covalent bonds, balancing equations, and reaction types.

questions.q: An ionic bond forms by:
questions.explain: Ionic bonds: electrons transfer, typically from a metal to a nonmetal.

questions.q: A covalent bond involves:
questions.explain: Covalent bonds share electron pairs between atoms.

questions.q: The chemical formula H₂O tells you each molecule has:
questions.explain: Subscripts count atoms: H₂O = two H, one O.

questions.q: In a balanced equation, atoms must be:
options: Equal in number on both sides
questions.explain: Conservation of mass: same atoms in, same atoms out.

questions.q: A reaction that releases heat is:
questions.explain: Exothermic reactions give off energy, usually as heat.

questions.q: The pH scale measures:
questions.explain: pH < 7 acidic, 7 neutral, > 7 basic.

questions.q: Which is a sign a chemical reaction occurred?
questions.explain: Color change, gas, precipitate, or temperature change signal a reaction.

questions.q: A catalyst speeds a reaction by:
questions.explain: Catalysts lower activation energy and are not consumed.

questions.q: Table salt (NaCl) is held together by which bond type?
questions.explain: Sodium transfers an electron to chlorine: a classic ionic compound.

questions.q: Water molecules stick to each other mainly through:
questions.explain: Hydrogen bonds between water molecules give water its cohesion.

rounds.title: Bonding & Reactions
rounds.desc: Ionic vs covalent bonds, balancing equations, and reaction types.

title: Acids, Bases & Solutions
subject: Chemistry 101
description: pH in daily life, neutralization, concentration, and mixtures.

questions.q: Pure water has a pH of:
questions.explain: pH 7 is neutral — pure water is neither acidic nor basic.

questions.q: Lemon juice, with a pH around 2, is:
questions.explain: pH below 7 means acidic.

questions.q: Mixing an acid and a base produces water and a salt in a ___ reaction.
questions.explain: Neutralization: acid + base → salt + water.

questions.q: The substance dissolved in a solution is the:
questions.explain: Solute dissolves in the solvent (the larger amount).

questions.q: In salt water, water is the:
questions.explain: Water does the dissolving, so it is the solvent.

questions.q: A solution that cannot dissolve any more solute at that temperature is:
questions.explain: Saturated = holding the maximum dissolved solute at equilibrium.

questions.q: Which would increase how fast a solid dissolves in water?
questions.explain: Stirring and more surface area speed dissolving.

questions.q: Baking soda is commonly used as a mild:
questions.explain: Sodium bicarbonate is a weak base — it neutralizes acids.

rounds.title: Acids, Bases & Solutions
rounds.desc: pH in daily life, neutralization, concentration, and mixtures.

title: Colonial Era & Revolution
subject: AP US History
description: Colonies, taxation, independence, and the Constitution.

questions.q: The Declaration of Independence was adopted in:
questions.explain: Adopted July 4, 1776, primarily authored by Thomas Jefferson.

questions.q: The British tax on printed materials that angered colonists was the:
questions.explain: The Stamp Act (1765) taxed printed goods and sparked 'no taxation without representation.'

questions.q: The first battles of the Revolutionary War were at:
questions.explain: Lexington and Concord, April 1775 — 'the shot heard round the world.'

questions.q: The Constitution was written in which year?
questions.explain: The Constitutional Convention met in Philadelphia in 1787.

questions.q: The Bill of Rights consists of the first ___ amendments.
questions.explain: The first ten amendments, ratified in 1791, protect individual liberties.

questions.q: The system that prevents any one branch from dominating is:
questions.explain: Checks and balances let each branch limit the others.

questions.q: The turning-point battle that convinced France to ally with America was:
questions.explain: Saratoga (1777) proved the Americans could win, bringing French support.

questions.q: The war effectively ended with the British surrender at:
questions.explain: Cornwallis surrendered at Yorktown in 1781.

title: Civil War & Reconstruction
subject: AP US History
description: Slavery, secession, emancipation, and rebuilding the Union.

questions.q: The Civil War began in:
questions.explain: Fighting began at Fort Sumter in April 1861.

questions.q: The Emancipation Proclamation freed enslaved people in:
questions.explain: Lincoln's 1863 proclamation applied to Confederate states in rebellion.

questions.q: Which amendment abolished slavery nationwide?
questions.explain: The 13th Amendment (1865) abolished slavery.

questions.q: The amendment granting citizenship and equal protection is the:
questions.explain: The 14th Amendment (1868) defines citizenship and equal protection.

questions.q: The bloodiest single day of the war was at:
questions.explain: Antietam (1862) remains the bloodiest single day in US military history.

questions.q: The Union general who accepted Lee's surrender was:
questions.explain: Ulysses S. Grant accepted the surrender at Appomattox in 1865.

questions.q: The 15th Amendment addressed:
questions.explain: Ratified 1870, it barred denying the vote based on race (for men).

questions.q: President Lincoln was assassinated in:
questions.explain: Lincoln was shot by John Wilkes Booth in April 1865, days after the war ended.

title: Great Depression & WWII
subject: AP US History
description: The crash, the New Deal, and America's path through World War II.

questions.q: The stock market crash that began the Great Depression occurred in:
questions.explain: Black Tuesday, October 29, 1929.

questions.q: Franklin D. Roosevelt's program to fight the Depression was the:
questions.explain: The New Deal brought relief, recovery, and reform programs.

questions.q: The attack that brought the US into WWII was on:
questions.explain: Japan attacked Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941.

questions.q: D-Day, the Allied invasion of Normandy, was in:
questions.explain: June 6, 1944 — the largest seaborne invasion in history.

questions.q: The Social Security Act was part of which program?
questions.explain: Passed in 1935 under the New Deal, it created old-age pensions.

questions.q: WWII in Europe ended in:
questions.explain: V-E Day was May 8, 1945.

questions.q: The US dropped atomic bombs on which two Japanese cities?
questions.explain: Hiroshima (Aug 6) and Nagasaki (Aug 9), 1945.

questions.q: The postwar US plan to rebuild Europe economically was the:
questions.explain: The Marshall Plan (1948) funded European recovery and contained communism.

title: High-Frequency Words A
subject: SAT Vocabulary
description: Core SAT words: meanings, roots, and usage.

questions.q: 'Meticulous' means:
questions.explain: Meticulous = showing great attention to detail.

questions.q: 'Ambiguous' means:
options: Open to more than one interpretation
questions.explain: Ambiguous language can be understood in multiple ways.

questions.q: To 'mitigate' a problem is to:
questions.explain: Mitigate = reduce the seriousness or impact.

questions.q: 'Pragmatic' describes someone who is:
questions.explain: Pragmatic people focus on what works in practice.

questions.q: 'Ephemeral' means:
questions.explain: Ephemeral things are fleeting — think a mayfly's lifespan.

questions.q: A 'candid' answer is:
questions.explain: Candid = truthful and straightforward.

questions.q: 'Diligent' means:
questions.explain: Diligent workers are steady, careful, and persistent.

questions.q: To 'refute' a claim is to:
questions.explain: Refute = disprove with evidence or argument.

questions.q: 'Superfluous' means:
questions.explain: Superfluous = more than what's needed.

questions.q: 'Tenacious' means:
questions.explain: Tenacious = not giving up easily.

title: High-Frequency Words B
subject: SAT Vocabulary
description: Second wave of essential SAT vocabulary.

questions.q: 'Aesthetic' relates to:
questions.explain: Aesthetics is the study of beauty and artistic taste.

questions.q: 'Benevolent' means:
questions.explain: A benevolent person is well-meaning and charitable.

questions.q: 'Coerce' means:
questions.explain: Coercion is persuasion by force or threats.

questions.q: 'Disdain' is:
questions.explain: To disdain is to regard something as beneath you.

questions.q: 'Eloquent' speech is:
questions.explain: Eloquent speakers express themselves powerfully and gracefully.

questions.q: 'Frugal' means:
questions.explain: A frugal person avoids waste and spends carefully.

questions.q: 'Gregarious' people are:
questions.explain: Gregarious = enjoys being around others.

questions.q: 'Hypothesis' is:
questions.explain: A hypothesis is an educated, testable prediction.

questions.q: 'Innovative' means:
questions.explain: Innovation = new methods or ideas.

questions.q: 'Juxtapose' means:
options: To place side by side for comparison
questions.explain: Juxtaposition contrasts two things by placing them together.

title: Roots & Prefixes
subject: SAT Vocabulary
description: Decode unfamiliar words by breaking them apart.

questions.q: The prefix 'bene-' (as in benefit) means:
questions.explain: Bene- comes from Latin for 'good/well.'

questions.q: The root 'chron' (chronology) relates to:
questions.explain: Chron- comes from Greek 'khronos,' time.

questions.q: 'Malfunction' — the prefix 'mal-' means:
questions.explain: Mal- = bad/wrongly, as in malice or malnutrition.

questions.q: The root 'bio' (biology) means:
questions.explain: Bio- comes from Greek 'bios,' life.

questions.q: 'Interstate' — the prefix 'inter-' means:

questions.q: The root 'scrib/script' (describe, manuscript) means:

questions.q: 'Submarine' — the prefix 'sub-' means:

title: Vital Signs & Patient Safety
subject: Nursing Fundamentals
description: Normal ranges, fall prevention, and the safety checks that matter.

questions.q: Normal adult resting heart rate is:
questions.explain: Normal adult resting pulse: 60–100 beats per minute.

questions.q: A normal adult oral temperature is about:
questions.explain: 98.6°F (37°C) is the standard average oral temperature.

questions.q: Blood pressure of 120/80 — the 120 represents:
questions.explain: The top number (systolic) is pressure during heart contraction.

questions.q: Normal adult respiratory rate is:
questions.explain: Adults normally breathe 12–20 times per minute at rest.

questions.q: Before giving any medication, the nurse first verifies:
questions.explain: Two identifiers (e.g., name + DOB) are required before medication administration.

questions.q: The best way to prevent falls in a hospitalized patient is to:
options: Keep the bed in high position
Keep the call light within reach and answer promptly
questions.explain: Call light access and prompt response are core fall-prevention measures.

questions.q: SpO₂ measures:
questions.explain: Pulse oximetry measures the percentage of hemoglobin carrying oxygen.

questions.q: A temperature of 101.5°F in an adult is considered:
questions.explain: Above 100.4°F is generally classified as a fever.

questions.q: When should hand hygiene be performed?
questions.explain: Hand hygiene before and after every patient contact is the standard.

questions.q: Bradycardia is a heart rate below:
questions.explain: Bradycardia = under 60 bpm; tachycardia = over 100 bpm.

title: Medication Administration
subject: Nursing Fundamentals
description: The rights of med administration, routes, and dosage safety.

questions.q: The traditional 'Five Rights' of medication administration include right patient, right drug, right dose, right route, and right:
questions.explain: The fifth right is the right time.

questions.q: The abbreviation 'PO' means a medication is given:
questions.explain: PO = per os, by mouth.

questions.q: 'IM' indicates an injection into the:
questions.explain: IM = intramuscular.

questions.q: A medication ordered 'STAT' should be given:
questions.explain: STAT means immediately, as soon as possible.

questions.q: Before administering a drug, the nurse should check for:
questions.explain: Allergy checking is a critical safety step for every medication.

questions.q: Sublingual medications are placed:
questions.explain: Sublingual = under the tongue for rapid absorption.

questions.q: If a patient refuses a medication, the nurse should:
options: Hide it in food without telling them
Document the refusal and notify the provider
questions.explain: Patients have the right to refuse; document it and inform the provider.

questions.q: The 'right documentation' means charting:
questions.explain: Document right after giving the medication — never before.

questions.q: Insulin is typically given by which route?
questions.explain: Insulin is given subcutaneously (into fatty tissue).

questions.q: A nurse finds a medication error was made. The priority action is:
options: Assess the patient and report per policy
questions.explain: Patient safety first: assess, then report and complete an incident report.

title: Infection Control
subject: Nursing Fundamentals
description: Chain of infection, precautions, and PPE essentials.

questions.q: The single most effective way to break the chain of infection is:
questions.explain: Hand hygiene is the #1 infection-prevention measure.

questions.q: Droplet precautions are used for infections spread by:
questions.explain: Droplets (flu, pertussis) travel short distances — mask and distance matter.

questions.q: Airborne precautions require which special mask?
questions.explain: Airborne diseases like TB require a fit-tested N95 and a negative-pressure room.

questions.q: Standard precautions apply to:
questions.explain: Standard precautions treat all blood/body fluids as potentially infectious, for every patient.

questions.q: The correct order for removing (doffing) PPE starts with:
questions.explain: Gloves are the most contaminated — remove them first, then goggles, gown, mask.

questions.q: Alcohol-based hand rub is NOT effective against:
questions.explain: C. diff spores require soap-and-water washing.

questions.q: Sharps containers should be replaced when they are:
questions.explain: Replace sharps containers at the fill line, about three-quarters full.

questions.q: Contact precautions require:
questions.explain: Contact precautions (e.g., MRSA, C. diff): gown + gloves when entering.

subject: Spanish Basics

questions.q: How do you say 'Good morning'?

questions.q: 'Hasta luego' means:

questions.q: The number 'seven' in Spanish is:

questions.q: 'Lo siento' means:

questions.q: 'Buenas noches' is used:

questions.q: 'Me llamo...' means:

subject: Spanish Basics

questions.q: 'Estoy cansado' means:

questions.q: 'Tener' means:

questions.q: 'Hablar' means:

questions.q: 'Comer' means:

questions.q: 'Vivir' means:

title: Learning & Conditioning
subject: Psychology 101
description: Pavlov, Skinner, Bandura — classical, operant, and observational learning.

questions.q: In Pavlov's experiment, the food is the:
questions.explain: Food naturally triggers salivation — it's unconditioned (unlearned).

questions.q: After pairing, the bell alone causing salivation means the bell is now a:
questions.explain: Once learned, the bell is the conditioned stimulus producing the conditioned response.

questions.q: Salivating to a similar-sounding tone as well as the trained bell is:
questions.explain: Generalization: responding to stimuli similar to the conditioned stimulus.

questions.q: Removing an aversive stimulus to INCREASE a behavior is:
questions.explain: Negative reinforcement strengthens behavior by taking something unpleasant away (seatbelt buzzer).

questions.q: A slot machine pays out after an unpredictable number of pulls. That's a ___ schedule.
questions.explain: Variable-ratio: reward after an unpredictable number of responses — high, steady responding.

questions.q: Paying a worker for every 10 items assembled is a ___ schedule.
questions.explain: Fixed-ratio: reinforcement after a set number of responses.

questions.q: Reinforcing closer and closer versions of a target behavior is called:
questions.explain: Shaping builds complex behavior by rewarding successive approximations.

questions.q: Bandura's Bobo doll study demonstrated:
questions.explain: Children imitated an aggressive model — learning by watching, especially when the model was rewarded.

questions.q: Tolman's rats learning a maze without rewards, then using it when rewards appear, showed:
questions.explain: Latent learning: knowledge acquired without obvious reinforcement, stored as a cognitive map.

questions.q: If a conditioned response fades when the CS is presented alone repeatedly, that's:
questions.explain: Extinction weakens the conditioned response when the CS no longer predicts the UCS.

title: Memory & Cognition
subject: Psychology 101
description: How memory is built, stored, lost — and the thinking shortcuts that misfire.

questions.q: Short-term memory holds about how many chunks of information?
questions.explain: Miller's famous 7±2 chunks — expandable by chunking related bits together.

questions.q: Visual sensory memory is called ___ memory; auditory is ___ memory.
questions.explain: Iconic = visual (~0.5s). Echoic = auditory (~3–4s).

questions.q: Memory for facts (capitals, definitions) is ___ memory; memory for personal events is ___.
questions.explain: Semantic = facts. Episodic = events from your life.

questions.q: Old learning interfering with recall of new learning is ___ interference.
questions.explain: Proactive: the OLD material pushes forward and blocks the new. Retroactive is the reverse.

questions.q: Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve shows forgetting is:
questions.explain: Most forgetting happens in the first hours — which is why early review matters so much.

questions.q: Judging how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind is the:
questions.explain: Availability: plane crashes feel common because vivid examples come to mind easily.

questions.q: Loftus's research showed that the wording of a question ('smashed' vs 'hit') can:
options: Alter memories and create false details
questions.explain: Memory is reconstructive — post-event information can be woven into what people 'remember.'

questions.q: Patient H.M. could learn new skills but not form new explicit memories, showing that:
options: Explicit and procedural memory are separate systems
questions.explain: H.M.'s pattern proved memory has distinct systems with different brain bases.

questions.q: Solving a problem by testing every possibility uses a(n):
questions.explain: Algorithms are exhaustive and guaranteed but slow; heuristics are fast shortcuts.

questions.q: The tendency to seek information confirming what you already believe is:
questions.explain: Confirmation bias: we search for, notice, and remember confirming evidence.

rounds.title: Memory & Cognition

title: Development Across the Lifespan
subject: Psychology 101
description: Piaget's stages, Erikson's crises, attachment, and moral development.

questions.q: A baby who searches for a toy hidden under a blanket has mastered:
questions.explain: Object permanence (~8 months, sensorimotor stage): things exist even when unseen.

questions.q: A child who thinks the taller glass must hold more juice lacks:
questions.explain: Conservation develops in the concrete operational stage; preoperational children center on one feature.

questions.q: Piaget's stage for abstract, hypothetical reasoning is:
questions.explain: Formal operational (12+): abstract and 'what if' thinking.

questions.q: Erikson's crisis for adolescents is:
questions.explain: Adolescence is about figuring out 'who am I?' — identity vs role confusion.

questions.q: Erikson's crisis in infancy is:
questions.explain: Consistent, responsive care in the first year builds basic trust.

questions.q: Harlow's monkeys preferred the cloth mother over the wire mother that fed them, proving attachment depends on:
questions.explain: Contact comfort, not feeding, drove attachment — a landmark result.

questions.q: In Ainsworth's Strange Situation, a baby who explores happily, is upset when mom leaves, and is soothed when she returns shows ___ attachment.
questions.explain: Secure attachment (~60–65%): the caregiver works as a secure base.

questions.q: Kohlberg's preconventional morality is based on:
questions.explain: Preconventional: right = what avoids punishment or gains reward.

questions.q: Vygotsky's term for what a child can do WITH help but not alone is the:
questions.explain: The ZPD is where good teaching aims — with scaffolding that fades as skill grows.

questions.q: Fitting a new experience into an existing schema is ___; changing the schema is ___.
questions.explain: Assimilation fits new into old; accommodation rebuilds the schema.

title: Brain & Biological Bases
subject: Psychology 101
description: Neurons, neurotransmitters, brain regions, and how we sense the world.

questions.q: The part of the neuron that RECEIVES signals from other neurons is the:
questions.explain: Dendrites receive; the axon sends. Myelin speeds the signal along the axon.

questions.q: The fatty coating that speeds neural impulses is the:
questions.explain: Myelin insulates the axon; its breakdown (as in MS) slows signaling.

questions.q: The junction where neurotransmitters cross between neurons is the:
questions.explain: The synapse is the tiny gap where chemical messages cross.

questions.q: Which neurotransmitter is most associated with reward and movement (and Parkinson's when lacking)?
questions.explain: Dopamine: reward, motivation, movement. Too little → Parkinson's symptoms.

questions.q: The brain area most responsible for forming new explicit memories is the:
questions.explain: The hippocampus consolidates explicit memories; the amygdala handles fear/emotion.

questions.q: Phineas Gage's personality changed after damage to his ___ lobe.
questions.explain: Frontal lobe damage altered Gage's planning and personality — a famous localization case.

questions.q: Broca's area damage causes difficulty ___; Wernicke's causes difficulty ___.
questions.explain: Broca = speech production. Wernicke = language comprehension.

questions.q: The sympathetic nervous system:
options: Is the same as the somatic system
questions.explain: Sympathetic = accelerator (fight/flight); parasympathetic = brake (rest/digest).

questions.q: The minimum stimulus strength detected 50% of the time is the:
questions.explain: Absolute threshold: the weakest detectable stimulus, half the time.

questions.q: Weber's law says the just-noticeable difference is a constant:
questions.explain: JND is proportional: 2% for weight — heavier objects need bigger absolute changes to notice.

title: Psychological Disorders & Therapy
subject: Psychology 101
description: DSM-5 categories, signature symptoms, and matching therapies to schools.

questions.q: Hallucinations and delusions are called ___ symptoms of schizophrenia.
questions.explain: Positive symptoms ADD experiences (hallucinations, delusions). Negative symptoms subtract (flat affect, avolition).

questions.q: Flat affect and loss of motivation in schizophrenia are ___ symptoms.
questions.explain: Negative symptoms are absences: flat affect, poverty of speech, avolition.

questions.q: OCD consists of obsessions, which are ___, and compulsions, which are ___.
questions.explain: Obsessions are intrusive thoughts; compulsions are rituals meant to neutralize them.

questions.q: A major depressive episode requires symptoms for at least:
questions.explain: Two weeks of depressed mood or anhedonia plus other symptoms marks a major depressive episode.

questions.q: Bipolar disorder involves depressive episodes alternating with:
questions.explain: Mania: elevated mood, racing thoughts, reduced need for sleep, risky behavior.

questions.q: Systematic desensitization — gradual exposure paired with relaxation — is a ___ therapy.
questions.explain: Wolpe's technique applies classical conditioning to unlearn fear.

questions.q: Unconditional positive regard is the signature condition of ___ therapy.
questions.explain: Rogers' client-centered therapy: unconditional positive regard, empathy, genuineness.

questions.q: Beck's cognitive therapy focuses on:
questions.explain: Cognitive therapy targets distorted thinking patterns that drive distress.

questions.q: A diagnosis of antisocial personality disorder requires the person to be at least:
questions.explain: ASPD requires age 18+ plus evidence of conduct disorder before age 15.

questions.q: The diathesis-stress model says disorders arise from:
questions.explain: Diathesis (predisposition) + stress = onset — the standard biopsychosocial explanation.

title: Human Body Systems
subject: Biology 101
description: Circulation, respiration, immunity, and homeostasis.

questions.q: Blood returning from the body enters the heart at the:
questions.explain: Body → right atrium → right ventricle → lungs → left atrium → left ventricle → body.

questions.q: Gas exchange in the lungs happens in the:
questions.explain: Alveoli are tiny air sacs wrapped in capillaries where O₂ and CO₂ diffuse.

questions.q: The protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen is:
questions.explain: Hemoglobin binds oxygen in the lungs and releases it in tissues.

questions.q: Vaccines work by:
options: Training memory cells before real infection
questions.explain: Vaccines present a harmless antigen so memory B/T cells are ready for the real pathogen.

questions.q: Homeostasis is maintained mainly through ___ feedback.
questions.explain: Negative feedback reverses a change (temperature, blood sugar). Positive feedback amplifies and is rare.

questions.q: Which organ filters blood and produces urine?
questions.explain: Kidneys filter blood, balance fluids, and form urine.

questions.q: Antibodies are produced by:
questions.explain: B cells mature into plasma cells that secrete antibodies against specific antigens.

questions.q: The diaphragm contracting causes you to:
questions.explain: The diaphragm flattens, expanding the chest, and air rushes in.

title: Microbes & Disease
subject: Biology 101
description: Bacteria vs viruses, transmission, and how we fight infection.

questions.q: Viruses differ from bacteria because viruses:
options: Are not alive and must hijack a host cell
questions.explain: Viruses are non-living particles of DNA/RNA in a protein coat — they need host cells to replicate.

questions.q: Antibiotics are effective against:
questions.explain: Antibiotics attack bacterial structures. They do nothing against viruses.

questions.q: Malaria is transmitted by a mosquito, making the mosquito a:
questions.explain: Vectors are organisms that carry pathogens between hosts.

questions.q: Binary fission is how ___ reproduce.
questions.explain: Bacteria copy their DNA and split into two — fast asexual reproduction.

questions.q: Quarantine applies to people who are ___; isolation applies to people who are ___.
questions.explain: Quarantine separates the exposed; isolation separates the ill.

questions.q: Which of these diseases is caused by a virus?
questions.explain: Influenza is viral; strep, TB, and cholera are bacterial.

questions.q: Antibiotic resistance develops mainly because:
questions.explain: Stopping early leaves the hardiest bacteria alive to multiply — selection in action.

questions.q: Pasteurization protects food by:
questions.explain: Pasteurization uses controlled heat to cut pathogen counts in milk and juices.

title: Matter & Measurement
subject: Chemistry 101
description: States of matter, physical vs chemical change, density, and sig figs.

questions.q: Dry ice turning directly into gas is:
questions.explain: Sublimation: solid → gas without becoming liquid.

questions.q: Melting ice is a ___ change.
questions.explain: Phase changes are physical — the substance (H₂O) is unchanged.

questions.q: Density is calculated as:
questions.explain: Density = mass/volume. Water's density is 1 g/mL.

questions.q: An object with density 0.6 g/mL placed in water will:
questions.explain: Less dense than water (1 g/mL) → it floats.

questions.q: How many significant figures are in 0.00450?
questions.explain: Leading zeros don't count; the trailing zero after 5 does: 4, 5, 0 = 3 sig figs.

questions.q: The metric prefix 'milli-' means:
questions.explain: Milli- = one thousandth (millimeter, milliliter).

questions.q: During a phase change, added heat:
options: Does not raise temperature until the change completes
questions.explain: The energy goes into breaking intermolecular attractions — temperature plateaus.

questions.q: A homogeneous mixture is also called a:
questions.explain: Solutions are homogeneous mixtures — uniform throughout.

title: Gilded Age & Progressives
subject: AP US History
description: Big business, labor, immigration, and the reform movements.

questions.q: Carnegie's steel empire used ___ integration — controlling every step from mines to mills.
questions.explain: Vertical integration controls the whole supply chain; Rockefeller's horizontal integration bought competitors.

questions.q: The Populist Party most strongly demanded:
questions.explain: Populists backed bimetallism ('free silver'), railroad regulation, and a graduated income tax.

questions.q: Upton Sinclair's 'The Jungle' led directly to:
options: Meat Inspection and Pure Food & Drug Acts (1906)
questions.explain: Sinclair exposed meatpacking horrors; Congress passed food-safety laws in 1906.

questions.q: The 17th Amendment established:
questions.explain: A Progressive reform — senators elected directly by voters, not state legislatures.

questions.q: The Spanish-American War (1898) resulted in the US gaining:
options: Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines
questions.explain: The Treaty of Paris gave the US Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines — an overseas empire.

questions.q: Jane Addams is associated with:
questions.explain: Hull House in Chicago provided services and reform energy in immigrant neighborhoods.

questions.q: The Chinese Exclusion Act (1882) was the first US law to:
options: Ban immigration by a specific nationality
questions.explain: It barred Chinese labor immigration — the first nationality-based exclusion.

questions.q: The Federal Reserve was created in 1913 under which president?
questions.explain: Wilson's New Freedom program created the Federal Reserve System.

title: Cold War & Modern America
subject: AP US History
description: Containment, civil rights, Vietnam, Watergate, and the conservative turn.

questions.q: The Truman Doctrine announced the US policy of:
questions.explain: Containment: stop Soviet/communist expansion — the Cold War's guiding strategy.

questions.q: Brown v. Board of Education (1954) ruled that:
questions.explain: The Court overturned 'separate but equal' in public education.

questions.q: The closest the US and USSR came to nuclear war was the:
questions.explain: Thirteen days in October 1962 over Soviet missiles in Cuba.

questions.q: The Civil Rights Act of 1964 banned:
options: Discrimination in public accommodations and employment
questions.explain: The 1964 act attacked segregation in public life and job discrimination.

questions.q: The Gulf of Tonkin Resolution (1964):
options: Gave LBJ broad war powers in Vietnam
questions.explain: Congress authorized escalation in Vietnam without a formal declaration of war.

questions.q: Watergate forced which president to resign?
questions.explain: Richard Nixon resigned in August 1974 — the only US president to do so.

questions.q: Medicare and Medicaid were created as part of:
questions.explain: LBJ's Great Society (1965): Medicare for seniors, Medicaid for low-income Americans.

questions.q: The Voting Rights Act of 1965:
options: Enabled federal enforcement of Black voting rights in the South
questions.explain: Federal examiners and preclearance finally made the 15th Amendment real in the South.

subject: SAT Vocabulary

questions.q: 'Arduous' means:
questions.explain: An arduous task demands real effort over time.

questions.q: In an academic article, a 'novel' approach is:

questions.q: 'Opaque' writing is:

questions.q: A 'prevalent' belief is:
questions.explain: Prevalent = common, widespread in a place or time.

questions.q: Someone 'reluctant' to speak is:
questions.explain: Reluctant = hesitant, not wanting to do it.

questions.q: To 'scrutinize' a document is to:
questions.explain: Scrutinize = inspect carefully and critically.

questions.q: A 'tedious' task is:
questions.explain: Tedious = tiresomely long or dull.

questions.q: Results that 'validate' a theory:
questions.explain: Validate = show to be sound or true.

questions.q: A 'versatile' tool can:

questions.q: A 'zealous' supporter is:
questions.explain: Zealous = filled with zeal — intense enthusiasm.

title: Pharmacology Basics
subject: Nursing Fundamentals
description: ADME, drug-class suffixes, and the antidotes every nurse knows.

questions.q: The 'M' in ADME (pharmacokinetics) stands for metabolism, which happens mainly in the:
questions.explain: The liver metabolizes most drugs; the kidneys excrete most.

questions.q: A drug's half-life is the time it takes for:
options: Half the drug to be eliminated
The drug to reach the brain
questions.explain: About 4–5 half-lives reach steady state or clear the drug.

questions.q: Drugs ending in '-lol' (metoprolol) are usually:
questions.explain: -lol = beta blocker: slows heart rate, lowers BP.

questions.q: Drugs ending in '-pril' (lisinopril) are:
questions.explain: -pril = ACE inhibitor; a dry cough is its classic side effect.

questions.q: The antidote for opioid overdose is:
questions.explain: Naloxone (Narcan) reverses opioids. Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines.

questions.q: Vitamin K is the antidote for:
questions.explain: Warfarin reversal = vitamin K. Heparin's antidote is protamine; acetaminophen's is N-acetylcysteine.

questions.q: IV medications have 100% bioavailability because they:
questions.explain: IV drugs go straight into circulation — nothing is lost to absorption or liver first pass.

questions.q: Digoxin toxicity is made worse by low levels of:
questions.explain: Hypokalemia increases digoxin binding and toxicity risk — vision changes and arrhythmias result.

subject: Spanish Basics
description: Getting around, describing people, family words, and possessives.

questions.q: 'A la derecha' means:
questions.explain: Derecha = right; izquierda = left; derecho/recto = straight.

questions.q: '¿Dónde está la estación?' asks:
questions.explain: Dónde está…? = Where is…? — the essential travel question.

questions.q: 'Cerca' means ___ and 'lejos' means ___.
questions.explain: Cerca = near, lejos = far.

questions.q: In the Universal Numbering System, tooth #1 is the:

questions.explain: Counting from #1 (upper right wisdom tooth), #8 is the maxillary right central incisor — the front tooth just right of the midline.

questions.explain: Adults have 32 permanent teeth: 8 incisors, 4 canines, 8 premolars, and 12 molars including the third molars (wisdom teeth). Primary dentition has 20 — no premolars and no third molars.

description: Caries progression, gum disease, abscesses, and the oral-cancer warning signs that demand a biopsy or referral.

questions.explain: A white spot lesion is subsurface enamel demineralization — chalky white and still reversible with fluoride and plaque control before a cavity (cavitation) forms.
questions.q: The earliest visible stage of tooth decay is a:

questions.explain: Streptococcus mutans ferments dietary sugars into acid; sustained acid drops plaque pH and dissolves enamel mineral — the core of the caries process.
questions.q: The bacterium most strongly linked to starting dental caries is:

questions.explain: Gingivitis is reversible inflammation with no permanent damage. Periodontitis adds irreversible clinical attachment loss and bone loss — the finding that changes the diagnosis.
options: Loss of attachment and alveolar bone
questions.q: What separates periodontitis from gingivitis?

questions.explain: When pulp tissue dies — usually from deep caries or trauma — bacteria exit the root apex and form a periapical abscess, seen as a radiolucency at the root tip.
questions.q: A periapical abscess most often develops from:

questions.explain: Leukoplakia is a clinical description, not a diagnosis: a white plaque that won't rub off and can't be attributed to another condition. Because some are precancerous, persistent lesions are biopsied.
options: Cannot be scraped off or diagnosed as another disease
questions.q: Leukoplakia is best defined as a white patch that:

questions.explain: Pseudomembranous candidiasis forms soft white plaques that wipe away to an erythematous (red) base — the wipe test is the quickest way to separate it from leukoplakia. It's common with dentures, recent antibiotics, and immune suppression.
options: Wipe off, leaving a red, raw surface
questions.q: Oral candidiasis (thrush) plaques typically:

questions.explain: Over 90% of oral cancers are squamous cell carcinomas arising from the surface epithelium; tobacco and alcohol are the dominant risk factors, with HPV driving many throat (oropharyngeal) cancers.
questions.q: The most common type of oral cancer is:

questions.explain: Any ulcer, lump, or red/white patch persisting beyond two weeks must be evaluated for malignancy — early oral cancers are often painless, so 'it doesn't hurt' is not reassuring.
options: A canker sore that heals in 10 days
An ulcer that has not healed after two weeks
A small traumatic bite mark from yesterday
questions.q: Which finding most urgently needs referral/biopsy?

questions.explain: Red lesions are rarer but far more dangerous: a large share of erythroplakias already show severe dysplasia or carcinoma at biopsy. High-risk sites include the lateral tongue and floor of the mouth.
options: Is always a burn from hot food
Has a higher rate of severe dysplasia/cancer than leukoplakia
questions.q: Erythroplakia (a red patch) is concerning because it:

questions.explain: Aphthae form inside the mouth on non-keratinized mucosa (inner cheeks, lips, tongue underside) and are not infectious; cold sores are herpes simplex, contagious, and typically crust on the lip border.
options: Are caused by herpes simplex virus
Occur on movable inner-mouth mucosa and are not contagious
questions.q: Recurrent aphthous ulcers (canker sores) differ from cold sores because they:

description: Lidocaine and articaine, infection antibiotics, endocarditis prophylaxis, and pain control — plus who needs caution.

questions.explain: 2% lidocaine with epinephrine is the workhorse: reliable onset, moderate duration, and the vasoconstrictor extends working time. Benzocaine is topical only — it numbs surface tissue before the injection.
questions.q: The most commonly used local anesthetic in dentistry is:

questions.explain: Epinephrine is a vasoconstrictor: less blood flow at the site means the anesthetic washes out more slowly (longer duration), with less bleeding and lower peak blood levels of the drug.
options: It constricts local blood vessels, prolonging anesthesia and reducing bleeding
It speeds up the onset to seconds
questions.q: Why is epinephrine added to local anesthetic solutions?

questions.explain: Pulling back the plunger checks for blood return — a positive aspiration means the needle tip is intravascular, and injecting there could cause rapid systemic effects like a racing heart from epinephrine.
options: Confirm the needle is not inside a blood vessel
questions.q: Before depositing anesthetic, the clinician aspirates mainly to:

questions.explain: Cardiac patients tolerate small, carefully aspirated doses, but epinephrine can raise heart rate and blood pressure — so the total dose is limited, or a plain anesthetic like 3% mepivacaine is chosen for short procedures.
options: Use unlimited amounts — it's only local
Limit the dose and consider a plain (no-epi) anesthetic
Use epinephrine only in the front teeth
questions.q: For a patient with significant cardiovascular disease, the safest approach to epinephrine is to:

questions.explain: Articaine's chemical structure gives it superior bone penetration, so a simple infiltration can sometimes numb lower molars where lidocaine usually needs a nerve block.
options: Diffuses through bone better than other amides
Is the only anesthetic safe in pregnancy
questions.q: Articaine 4% is often chosen for mandibular teeth because it:

questions.explain: Amoxicillin covers the mixed oral flora of a dental abscess well and is first-line. Antibiotics support — never replace — draining the infection and treating the tooth itself.
questions.q: The first-line antibiotic for a typical odontogenic (tooth) infection in a non-allergic adult is:

questions.explain: Clindamycin is the classic alternative for penicillin-allergic patients because it covers oral anaerobes and streptococci without the penicillin ring.
questions.q: A patient with a true penicillin allergy who needs an antibiotic for a dental infection is typically prescribed:

questions.explain: Per AHA guidance, high-risk cardiac patients take a single 2 g amoxicillin dose shortly before the appointment so blood levels peak during the procedure's brief bacteremia. Clindamycin 600 mg is the classic alternative for penicillin allergy.
options: Amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for a week
Amoxicillin 2 g by mouth, single dose 30–60 minutes before the procedure
An antibiotic started the day after treatment
questions.q: Standard antibiotic prophylaxis against infective endocarditis before invasive dental work (for high-risk patients) is:

questions.explain: Ibuprofen (an NSAID) blocks prostaglandin production, attacking the inflammation causing the pain; acetaminophen relieves pain centrally but has almost no anti-inflammatory effect — the two are often combined for stronger relief.
options: It is anti-inflammatory, and most dental pain is driven by inflammation
questions.q: Why is ibuprofen usually preferred over acetaminophen for post-extraction pain?

questions.explain: NSAIDs reduce the prostaglandins that protect the stomach lining and support kidney blood flow, so ulcer history, chronic kidney disease, and anticoagulant use are the classic cautions.
options: A history of stomach ulcers or kidney disease
questions.q: NSAIDs like ibuprofen should be used cautiously or avoided in patients with:

description: Amalgam vs composite, glass ionomer, luting cements, and impression materials — picking the right material for the job.

questions.explain: Amalgam forms when liquid mercury is mixed (triturated) with a silver–tin–copper alloy powder; the set material is strong and durable, especially under heavy back-tooth chewing loads.
questions.q: Dental amalgam is an alloy of mercury combined mainly with:

questions.explain: Composite bonds to etched enamel and dentin, so the dentist removes less healthy tooth than amalgam's mechanical-retention shapes require — and it's tooth-colored.
options: Bonds adhesively to tooth structure, allowing more conservative preparations
Sets without any light or mixing
questions.q: A key advantage of composite resin over amalgam is that it:

questions.explain: Glass ionomer chemically bonds to tooth and slowly releases fluoride, making it a favorite for root-surface lesions, pediatric fillings, and high-caries-risk patients — though it's weaker than composite.
options: Releases fluoride and bonds chemically to tooth structure
questions.q: Glass ionomer cement is especially valued in dentistry because it:

questions.explain: Eugenol is a free-radical scavenger, so residual ZOE under a composite restoration can prevent the resin from curing properly — a classic materials-compatibility exam point.
options: Inhibits the polymerization (setting) of composite resin
questions.q: Zinc oxide–eugenol (ZOE) is known for its soothing effect on the pulp, but its eugenol:

questions.explain: Zinc phosphate holds crowns by mechanical interlocking into microscopic irregularities; it is strong in compression but has zero chemical adhesion and is acidic when freshly mixed.
options: Retains crowns mechanically and has no true adhesion to tooth
questions.q: Zinc phosphate cement, one of the oldest luting cements:

questions.explain: Its polyacrylic acid chains bond to calcium in the tooth, and it's notably kind to the pulp — a gentler, adhesive alternative to zinc phosphate.
questions.q: Polycarboxylate cement was historically important because it was the first cement to:

questions.explain: Alginate (irreversible hydrocolloid) is cheap and easy but dimensionally unstable — it gains and loses water fast, so casts must be poured within minutes for accuracy.
options: Study models — and it must be poured promptly
questions.q: Alginate impression material is best used for:

questions.explain: PVS captures fine detail and stays dimensionally stable for days, unlike alginate — which is why it's the standard for definitive restorative impressions.
questions.q: For a final crown-and-bridge impression, the most accurate, stable choice is:

questions.explain: Calcium hydroxide's high pH mildly irritates the pulp in a controlled way, prompting odontoblasts to lay down a reparative dentin bridge over a near-exposure.
options: Stimulates the pulp to form reparative (secondary) dentin
questions.q: Calcium hydroxide liner (e.g., Dycal) is placed in deep preparations because it:

questions.explain: Acid etching dissolves enamel rod ends, creating a frosted, high-energy surface full of micro-undercuts; resin tags lock into these, giving composite its bond strength.
options: Create microscopic pores that resin flows into for micromechanical retention
Kill all bacteria in the dentin
questions.q: Enamel is etched with phosphoric acid (about 37%) before bonding in order to:

description: Probing depths, attachment loss, Stage I–IV periodontitis, scaling and root planing, and maintenance intervals.

questions.explain: Probing depths of 1–3 mm with no bleeding indicate health; deeper readings suggest a periodontal pocket has formed as attachment migrates down the root.
questions.q: A healthy gingival sulcus typically probes at:

questions.explain: CAL uses the fixed CEJ landmark: probing depth plus gingival recession (when the margin sits below the CEJ). It measures total support lost, which pocket depth alone can hide.
options: The gumline to the base of the pocket
The cementoenamel junction (CEJ) to the base of the pocket
The crown tip to the root tip
The bone crest to the apex
questions.q: Clinical attachment loss (CAL) is measured from:

questions.explain: Inflamed pocket epithelium is thin and ulcerated, so gentle probing provokes bleeding; absence of bleeding is a strong sign of periodontal stability.
questions.q: Bleeding on probing at a site indicates:

questions.explain: Staging runs by worst-site attachment loss: Stage I = 1–2 mm, Stage II = 3–4 mm, Stage III/IV = 5 mm or more, with increasing tooth-loss risk and treatment complexity.
questions.q: Under the current staging system, Stage I periodontitis shows interdental CAL of about:

questions.explain: Stage II is moderate periodontitis — 3–4 mm of attachment loss and radiographic bone loss into the coronal third of the root (roughly 15–33%).
questions.q: Stage II periodontitis corresponds to interdental CAL of:

questions.explain: SRP is the cornerstone nonsurgical therapy for periodontitis: thorough subgingival debridement so the gum can heal against a clean, smooth root and pocket depths shrink.
options: A cosmetic polish above the gumline
Nonsurgical deep cleaning that removes calculus and smooths root surfaces below the gumline
questions.q: Scaling and root planing (SRP) is best described as:

questions.explain: Periodontal pathogens recolonize pockets within weeks; the classic 3–4 month maintenance interval keeps bacterial loads below the threshold that restarts attachment loss.
questions.q: After active periodontal therapy, supportive maintenance visits are typically scheduled every:

questions.explain: Smoking impairs blood flow and immune defense in the gums and blunts healing — smokers lose more attachment and respond worse to treatment; it also masks bleeding, hiding disease.
questions.q: The strongest modifiable risk factor for periodontitis is:

questions.explain: Poorly controlled diabetes accelerates periodontal destruction, and periodontal inflammation in turn worsens insulin resistance and glycemic control — treating one helps the other.
questions.q: The relationship between diabetes and periodontitis is:

questions.explain: When attachment loss reaches the fork between molar roots, cleaning becomes difficult and prognosis drops — furcation involvement is a key finding on molars.
options: Bone loss has entered the area where a multirooted tooth's roots divide
questions.q: Furcation involvement means:

description: Reversible vs irreversible pulpitis, necrosis, periapical diagnosis, apex locators, and obturation with gutta-percha.

questions.explain: A brief, sharp response that fades = reversible pulpitis (the pulp can recover). Lingering or spontaneous pain means the inflamed pulp cannot recover — irreversible pulpitis, treated with root canal therapy or extraction.
questions.q: Pain that lingers for 30+ seconds after a cold stimulus is removed suggests:

questions.explain: If the pulp can recover, conservative care — removing caries or leaky restorations and sealing the tooth — lets inflammation resolve; no endodontic treatment is needed.
options: Removing the irritant (e.g., replacing the leaking filling) and monitoring
questions.q: Reversible pulpitis is typically treated by:

questions.explain: A dead pulp can't respond: necrosis is the usual finding, though multirooted teeth can have mixed status and recently traumatized teeth can give false negatives, so results are confirmed with other tests.
questions.q: A tooth that gives NO response to cold testing or electric pulp testing most likely has:

questions.explain: Percussion tenderness localizes inflammation to the periodontal ligament around the root apex — a hallmark of apical periodontitis, often from a dying pulp or a high bite.
questions.q: Pain on biting or percussion of a tooth points to inflammation in the:

questions.explain: Apex locators sense when a file reaches the apical constriction/foramen, letting the clinician set working length accurately (confirmed with a radiograph) and avoid over-instrumenting.
options: Determine the working length by locating the apical constriction
questions.q: An electronic apex locator is used during root canal therapy to:

questions.explain: Sodium hypochlorite dissolves organic tissue and kills bacteria inside the canal system — functions no file can accomplish in fins and lateral canals.
questions.q: The primary irrigant used to clean root canals is:

questions.explain: Gutta-percha — a rubbery, biocompatible material — is compacted with sealer to three-dimensionally fill and seal the cleaned canal space against re-infection.
questions.q: Canals are obturated (filled) primarily with:

questions.explain: The dam prevents saliva (and its bacteria) from contaminating the canal and stops small files or caustic irrigant from being swallowed or aspirated — a clinical and legal standard of care.
options: It isolates the tooth, keeping the canal aseptic and protecting the airway from instruments/irrigants
It is only for patient comfort
questions.q: Why is a rubber dam mandatory for root canal treatment?

questions.explain: RCT follows a fixed logic: enter the pulp chamber, measure each canal, disinfect and shape, seal with gutta-percha, then protect the tooth — usually with a crown on back teeth.
options: Access opening → determine working length → clean & shape → obturate → restore the crown
Fill the crown → drill the root
questions.q: In sequence, the major steps of root canal therapy are:

questions.explain: Chronic apical periodontitis destroys bone at the apex, producing the classic periapical radiolucency; treating the canal source usually allows the bone to heal.
options: A periapical lesion (bone lost to inflammation from the necrotic pulp)
questions.q: A dark (radiolucent) circle at the tip of a root on a radiograph, in a non-vital tooth, most likely represents:

description: Bitewing vs periapical vs panoramic, ALARA, shielding, digital imaging, and reading radiolucent vs radiopaque.

questions.explain: Bitewings show the crowns of upper and lower teeth together with the alveolar crest — ideal geometry for spotting decay between teeth and early bone loss.
options: Interproximal (between-the-teeth) caries and crestal bone levels
questions.q: Bitewing radiographs are the best choice for detecting:

questions.explain: The PA is the diagnostic image for the whole tooth — apex included — which is why it's used for abscesses, root fractures, and endodontic working lengths.
options: The entire tooth from crown tip to root apex plus surrounding bone
questions.q: A periapical (PA) radiograph shows:

questions.explain: Panoramic images trade fine detail for coverage: both jaws in one shot for wisdom teeth, large lesions, fractures, and growth assessment — but never for fine caries diagnosis.
options: A broad overview — impacted third molars, jaw lesions, trauma, and development
questions.q: A panoramic image is most useful for:

questions.explain: ALARA means every exposure must be justified and optimized — take only images that change care, and use fast receptors, collimation, and correct technique to keep dose minimal.
questions.q: ALARA, the guiding principle of dental radiography, stands for:

questions.explain: Lead shielding absorbs scatter; the thyroid collar matters because the thyroid is radiation-sensitive — especially in children — and sits close to the beam path.
options: Shield the patient's torso and thyroid from scatter radiation
questions.q: During radiography, the lead apron and thyroid collar serve to:

questions.explain: Digital sensors are more sensitive than film, cutting dose significantly, and images appear immediately, can be enhanced, and are stored electronically — no darkroom chemistry.
options: Uses less radiation and produces images instantly without chemicals
questions.q: Compared with traditional film, digital radiography generally:

questions.explain: Radiolucent = X-rays pass through easily, exposing the receptor more → dark. Soft tissue, pulp, decay, and abscesses are radiolucent; dense structures block rays and appear light.
questions.q: On a radiograph, a radiolucent structure appears:

questions.explain: Radiopacity tracks density: enamel is the most mineralized tissue in the body and metals block nearly all radiation, so both image bright white against darker dentin and bone.
options: Enamel and metallic restorations like amalgam
questions.q: Which of these appears most radiopaque (bright white) on a radiograph?

questions.explain: When receptor and tooth are parallel and the beam is aimed at right angles to both, the image is dimensionally accurate — critical for endodontic measurements.
options: Produces the least distortion by keeping the receptor parallel to the tooth and the beam perpendicular
Uses half the radiation of any other method
questions.q: The paralleling technique is preferred for periapical images because it:

questions.explain: Routine images are deferred, but a needed diagnostic image (with apron/collar and modern low-dose technique) delivers negligible fetal exposure and should not be withheld in an emergency.
options: Take a full series at every visit
Postpone elective images; take only diagnostically necessary ones with shielding
Never take any image under any circumstance, even emergencies
questions.q: For a pregnant patient, the standard approach to dental radiographs is to:
